propositions.text: Applicant Marsel Idrizi is a 28-year-old Albanian citizen who claimed refugee protection in Canada in 2012, rejected in 2014, but stayed on work permits.
propositions.quote: The applicant, Marsel Idrizi, is a twenty-eight year old citizen of Albania. After arriving in Canada in January 2012, he made a claim for refugee protection. This claim was rejected in March 2014 but Mr. Idrizi remained in Canada on a series of work permits.

paragraphs.summary: The court states that applicant Marsel Idrizi is a 28-year-old Albanian who claimed refugee protection in 2012, rejected in 2014, but stayed on work permits.

propositions.text: In June 2016, Idrizi married Valbona Ruko, also 28 and Albanian, who became a Canadian permanent resident six months earlier.
propositions.quote: In June 2016, Mr. Idrizi married Valbona Ruko in Vaughan, Ontario. Ms. Ruko, who is also a twenty-eight year old citizen of Albania, had become a permanent resident of Canada about six months earlier.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Idrizi married Valbona Ruko in June 2016, who was also 28, Albanian, and a Canadian permanent resident for six months.

propositions.text: In August 2016, Ruko applied to sponsor Idrizi for permanent residence as spouse/common-law partner; she was pregnant and gave birth in February 2017.
propositions.quote: In August 2016, Ms. Ruko applied to sponsor Mr. Idrizi for permanent residence as a member of the spouse or common law partner living in Canada class. At the time of the application, Ms. Ruko was pregnant. She gave birth to a daughter in February 2017.

propositions.text: No suggestion that Idrizi is not the father of the child.
propositions.quote: There is no suggestion that Mr. Idrizi is not the father.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Ruko applied to sponsor Idrizi in August 2016 while pregnant; she gave birth in February 2017 and Idrizi is presumed father.

propositions.text: IRCC officer refused permanent residence application because couple failed to prove marriage was genuine and not primarily for immigration status.
propositions.quote: In a decision dated August 27, 2018, an officer with Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada [IRCC] refused the application for permanent residence because Mr. Idrizi and Ms. Ruko failed to establish that they had not entered into their marriage primarily for the purpose of acquiring any status or privilege under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 [IRPA] and that their marriage is genuine.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker refused Idrizi's permanent residence application for failing to prove marriage genuineness and not for immigration status.

propositions.text: Idrizi applies for judicial review of the IRCC officer's decision under section 72(1) of IRPA.
propositions.quote: Mr. Idrizi now applies for judicial review of this decision under section 72(1) of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant applies for judicial review of the officer's decision under IRPA section 72(1).

propositions.text: The officer's decision is unreasonable; judicial review is allowed and matter remitted for redetermination.
propositions.quote: For the reasons that follow, I have concluded that the officer’s decision is unreasonable. The application for judicial review will, therefore, be allowed and the matter will be remitted to another officer for redetermination.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the officer's decision is unreasonable, allows judicial review, and remits the matter for redetermination.

propositions.text: Idrizi was born in Albania in 1991, arrived in Canada in 2012, claimed refugee protection as a gay man fearing persecution, rejected in 2014, and judicial review dismissed in 2015.
propositions.quote: Mr. Idrizi was born in Albania in February 1991. He arrived in Canada on January 20, 2012. The next day he made a claim for refugee protection on the basis that, as a gay man, he feared persecution in Albania. For reasons released on March 25, 2014, the Refugee Protection Division of the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada determined that Mr. Idrizi is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. An application for judicial review of this decision was dismissed by Justice Tremblay-Lamer on May 15, 2015 (Court File No. IMM-2793-14).

paragraphs.summary: The court states Idrizi was born in 1991, claimed refugee protection in 2012 as a gay man, rejected in 2014, and judicial review dismissed in 2015.

propositions.text: Idrizi and Ruko first met at a party in January 2015, initially friends, romantically involved by June 2015.
propositions.quote: According to Mr. Idrizi and Ms. Ruko, the two first met at a party in January 2015. At first they were just friends but by June 2015 they had become romantically involved.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant states he and Ruko met in January 2015, were friends, and became romantically involved by June 2015.

propositions.text: Ruko sought refugee protection as a lesbian fearing persecution; her claim was accepted and she became permanent resident in December 2015.
propositions.quote: Ms. Ruko had also sought refugee protection in Canada on the basis of sexual orientation. She claimed that, as a lesbian, she feared persecution in Albania. Her claim, however, was accepted. She became a permanent resident of Canada on December 7, 2015.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant states Ruko sought refugee protection as a lesbian, was accepted, and became permanent resident in December 2015.

propositions.text: Idrizi and Ruko decided to live together, rented apartment in Etobicoke from March 2016, married June 2016, had honeymoon trips, and Ruko became pregnant and gave birth in February 2017.
propositions.quote: Mr. Idrizi and Ms. Ruko state that they decided to live together. They rented an apartment in Etobicoke beginning March 1, 2016. Both of their names were on the lease. They were married in June 2016. About 100 guests attended the wedding. Mr. Idrizi and Ms. Ruko went to Montreal, Mont-Tremblant and Niagara Falls for their honeymoon. A short time later, Ms. Ruko learned that she was pregnant. She gave birth to a daughter in February 2017. Both Ms. Ruko and Mr. Idrizi are named as the parents on the Statement of Live Birth form.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant states they lived together from March 2016, married June 2016, honeymooned, and had a child in February 2017 with both named parents.

propositions.text: An officer initially reviewing the permanent residence application required further investigation due to refugee claim grounds related to sexual orientation.
propositions.quote: The application for permanent residence for Mr. Idrizi was submitted in August 2016. When it was reviewed, an officer (not the one who made the decision) determined that, given the grounds that had been advanced in the refugee claims – Mr. Idrizi is gay, Ms. Ruko is a lesbian – further investigation of their relationship was required.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker states an officer required further investigation of the relationship due to refugee claim grounds.

propositions.text: Idrizi and Ruko were called for an interview on August 8, 2018; decision rejecting application followed shortly after.
propositions.quote: By email sent on July 24, 2018, Mr. Idrizi and Ms. Ruko were called in for an interview on August 8, 2018. The decision rejecting the application was made a short time later.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker states the couple was interviewed August 8, 2018, and the refusal decision followed soon after.

propositions.text: Section 124 of IRPR defines spouse/common-law partner in Canada class by cohabitation, temporary resident status, and sponsorship application.
propositions.quote: Section 124 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, SOR/2002-227 [IRPR] provides that a foreign national is a member of the spouse or common-law partner in Canada class if they: (a) are the spouse or common-law partner of a sponsor and cohabit with their spouse in Canada; (b) have temporary resident status in Canada; and (c) are the subject of a sponsorship application.

paragraphs.summary: The court states section 124 IRPR defines spouse/common-law partner class by cohabitation, temporary status, and sponsorship application.

propositions.text: Only paragraph 124(a) of IRPR is in issue here.
propositions.quote: Only paragraph 124(a) of the IRPR is in issue here.

paragraphs.summary: The court states only paragraph 124(a) of IRPR is at issue.

propositions.text: Section 4(1) IRPR excludes spouses if marriage is primarily for immigration status or not genuine.
propositions.quote: 4 (1) For the purposes of these Regulations, a foreign national shall not be considered a spouse, a common-law partner or a conjugal partner of a person if the marriage, common-law partnership or conjugal partnership 4 (1) Pour l’application du présent règlement, l’étranger n’est pas considéré comme étant l’époux, le conjoint de fait ou le partenaire conjugal d’une personne si le mariage ou la relation des conjoints de fait ou des partenaires conjugaux, selon le cas : (a) was entered into primarily for the purpose of acquiring any status or privilege under the Act; or a) visait principalement l’acquisition d’un statut ou d’un privilège sous le régime de la Loi; (b) is not genuine. b) n’est pas authentique. […] […]

paragraphs.summary: The court states section 4(1) IRPR excludes spouses if marriage is primarily for immigration status or not genuine.

propositions.text: At interview, officer cited section 4(1) IRPR and questioned couple separately and together about daily routines and family contacts, noting discrepancies.
propositions.quote: At the interview on August 8, 2018, the officer drew section 4(1) of the IRPR to the attention of Mr. Idrizi and Ms. Ruko. The officer then questioned them separately and, later on, together about a number of things including daily routines, things that had happened the day before the interview and the morning of the interview, how often the other person was in contact with his/her parents or other family and whether Mr. Idrizi had met Ms. Ruko’s parents. While many of their answers were in accord, the officer noted several discrepancies that were then put to Mr. Idrizi and to Ms. Ruko for comment.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker states the officer cited section 4(1) IRPR and questioned the couple about routines and family, noting discrepancies.

propositions.text: Officer noted eight specific discrepancies between Idrizi and Ruko's interview answers about addresses, arrival times, family contacts, and visits.
propositions.quote: Eight of these discrepancies were noted specifically in the officer’s decision: (a) Ms. Ruko’s driver’s licence showed the Etobicoke address where the couple said they both had lived since March 2016 but Mr. Idrizi’s driver’s licence (which had been issued in April 2017) showed an address in Waterloo, Ontario.Mr. Idrizi presented the officer with a change of address form dated July 26, 2018, changing the address on his driver’s licence to the Etobicoke address.He explained that he had used a false address for his driver’s licence so that he could get a better rate on his car insurance.Insurance documents provided by Mr. Idrizi indicated that the Waterloo address was used for his car insurance.However, the documents also indicated that Mr. Idrizi had been paying for home insurance for the Waterloo address since at least August 2017.(On the other hand, many other documents showed the Etobicoke apartment as his home address.) (b) Mr. Idrizi said he would usually get home from work around 7:00 to 7:30 p.m.Ms. Ruko said he would usually get home around 5:00 to 6:00 p.m. (c) Mr. Idrizi said he had arrived home the night before at around 6:00 p.m.Ms. Ruko said he had come home at 7:30 p.m. (d) Mr. Idrizi said Ms. Ruko only has contact with her mother.Ms. Ruko said she is in contact with both her parents over Skype. (e) Mr. Idrizi said Ms. Ruko’s parents have not come to Canada.Ms. Ruko said they had. (f) Mr. Idrizi said he had not met Ms. Ruko’s parents.Ms. Ruko said that her mother had been in Canada from February 2017 until the end of July 2017 (for the birth of the baby) and that both her parents had come from December 2017 until June 2018.Mr. Idrizi had met them when they were visiting. (g) Mr. Idrizi said he only has contact with his mother and not with his father.Ms. Ruko said he communicates with his family on Skype and Facebook and that his father calls him from time to time (something Mr. Idrizi later acknowledged but then added that he and his father do not get along). (h) Mr. Idrizi said he and Ms. Ruko had last seen Ms. Ruko’s Uncle Hasbee when he came to visit them at their house the previous Wednesday.Ms. Ruko said they had last seen him at their house the previous Saturday.When this discrepancy was pointed out to Mr. Idrizi, he agreed with Ms. Ruko.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker notes eight discrepancies in the couple's interview answers about addresses, times, family contacts, and visits.

propositions.text: Couple provided documentation including child's birth certificate listing both as parents; child was present at interview though not mentioned in decision.
propositions.quote: The officer noted that Mr. Idrizi and Ms. Ruko had “provided a variety of documentation and information to support their cohabitation and relationship, including a birth certificate for a child for which [sic] they are both listed as a parent.” (While not mentioned in the decision, there is no dispute that the child was at the interview with her parents.)

propositions.text: Officer found documentation did not outweigh interview information; existence of child not determinative of positive decision.
propositions.quote: The officer found, however, that this information did not outweigh the information presented at the interview. The officer added: “The existence of a child is not determinative of a positive decision as it is essential that the PA [Principal Applicant – Mr. Idrizi] and SPR [Sponsor – Ms. Ruko] meet the requirements of the class.”

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker notes couple provided documents including child's birth certificate but found interview info outweighed them; child existence not determinative.

propositions.text: Officer concluded on balance of probabilities that couple's relationship is not genuine and entered primarily for immigration status.
propositions.quote: The officer concluded as follows: After reviewing all the evidence provided, on a balance of probabilities, I am not satisfied that the PA and SPR are in a genuine spousal relationship and not one entered into primarily for the purpose of acquiring any status or privilege under the Act. I come to this conclusion based on an overall assessment of the documentary evidence, and the information provided by the PA and SPR during their interviews.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker concluded on balance of probabilities that the couple's relationship is not genuine and entered primarily for immigration status.

propositions.text: Idrizi was excluded from spouse/common-law partner class under section 4(1) IRPR; permanent residence application refused.
propositions.quote: Since Mr. Idrizi was therefore not considered a spouse under section 4(1) of the IRPR, he was excluded from the spouse or common law partner in Canada class as defined by paragraph 124(a) of the IRPR. The application for permanent residence was refused as a result.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker excluded Idrizi from spouse class under section 4(1) IRPR and refused permanent residence application.

propositions.text: Decisions on permanent residence applications under spouse/common law partner class are reviewed on a reasonableness standard.
propositions.quote: It is well-established that decisions on applications for permanent residence under the spouse or common law partner living in Canada class are reviewed on a reasonableness standard.

propositions.text: Whether a marriage is genuine or for immigration is a factual inquiry entitled to deference, especially if decision-maker questioned spouses in person.
propositions.quote: Whether a marriage was entered into primarily for the purpose of immigration or is genuine is a highly factual inquiry and decision-makers are entitled to deference from reviewing courts. This is particularly the case when the decision-maker has the benefit of having questioned the spouses in person

paragraphs.summary: The court states that spouse class permanent residence decisions are reviewed for reasonableness, with deference to decision-makers who questioned spouses in person.

propositions.text: Reasonableness review concerns substantive outcome and articulation process of decision.
propositions.quote: Reasonableness review “is concerned with the reasonableness of the substantive outcome of the decision, and with the process of articulating that outcome”

propositions.text: Reviewing court examines justification, transparency, intelligibility, and whether decision falls within acceptable outcomes range.
propositions.quote: The reviewing court examines the decision for “the existence of justification, transparency and intelligibility within the decision-making process” and determines “whether the decision falls within a range of possible, acceptable outcomes which are defensible in respect of the facts and law”

propositions.text: Reasons must allow court to understand decision and determine if conclusion is acceptable.
propositions.quote: These criteria are met if “the reasons allow the reviewing court to understand why the tribunal made its decision and permit it to determine whether the conclusion is within the range of acceptable outcomes”

propositions.text: Court should intervene only if criteria not met; not to reweigh evidence or substitute opinion.
propositions.quote: The reviewing court should intervene only if these criteria are not met. It is not the role of the reviewing court to reweigh the evidence or to substitute its opinion for that of the original decision-maker

paragraphs.summary: The court explains reasonableness review requires justification, transparency, intelligibility, and defers to original decision-maker's findings.

propositions.text: Mr. Idrizi contended officer breached procedural fairness by not putting discrepancies to him or Ms. Ruko.
propositions.quote: Mr. Idrizi also contended that the officer breached the requirements of procedural fairness by failing to put the discrepancies which grounded the decision to him or to Ms. Ruko.

propositions.text: Record shows concerns were fairly put to Mr. Idrizi and Ms. Ruko.
propositions.quote: A review of the record demonstrates that the concerns were fairly put to them.

propositions.text: Procedural fairness issue not pressed at hearing and need not be considered further given outcome.
propositions.quote: The issue of procedural fairness was not pressed at the hearing of this matter and, in view of the outcome, there is no need to consider it further.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argued procedural fairness breach; court finds concerns were fairly put and declines further consideration.

propositions.text: Officer found Mr. Idrizi disqualified under section 4(1) IRPR for not being in genuine spousal relationship and marriage entered primarily for immigration.
propositions.quote: The officer found that Mr. Idrizi was disqualified from the spouse or common law partner living in Canada class under section 4(1) of the IRPR. Specifically, the officer was not satisfied that Mr. Idrizi and Ms. Ruko “are in a genuine spousal relationship and not one entered into primarily for the purpose of acquiring any status or privilege under the Act.”

propositions.text: Officer based conclusion on documentary evidence and interview information.
propositions.quote: This conclusion, the officer explained, was “based on an overall assessment of the documentary evidence, and the information provided by the PA and SPR during their interviews.”

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found the applicant disqualified under section 4(1) IRPR based on documentary and interview evidence.

propositions.text: Current section 4(1) IRPR version came into force Sept 30, 2010, replacing previous version.
propositions.quote: As has been discussed elsewhere ... the current version of section 4(1) of the IRPR came into force on September 30, 2010

propositions.text: Previous version required marriage to be both not genuine and entered primarily for immigration to disqualify.
propositions.quote: The version it replaced read as follows: 4. For the purposes of these Regulations, a foreign national shall not be considered a spouse ... if the marriage ... is not genuine and was entered into primarily for the purpose of acquiring any status or privilege under the Act.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the current section 4(1) IRPR replaced a previous version requiring both non-genuineness and immigration purpose to disqualify.

propositions.text: Material change: test changed from conjunctive to disjunctive for disqualification under section 4(1) IRPR.
propositions.quote: For present purposes, the material change in the provision is that what had been a conjunctive test for disqualification is now a disjunctive test.

propositions.text: Previously, both non-genuine and immigration purpose had to be found; rebuttable presumption existed that non-genuine implied immigration purpose.
propositions.quote: Previously, to disqualify spousal status under this provision, a decision-maker had to determine both that the marriage was not genuine and that it was entered into primarily for an immigration purpose. The two elements are closely connected so it is not surprising that a rebuttable presumption that a non-genuine marriage was entered into primarily for an immigration purpose emerged under the previous version

propositions.text: Previous version would not disqualify marriage entered primarily for immigration but later genuine.
propositions.quote: Conversely, however, the previous version of section 4(1) would not disqualify a marriage that had been entered into primarily for an immigration purpose but which had later grown into a genuine relationship

propositions.text: Amended provision intended to make disqualification decision more straightforward.
propositions.quote: By making the test disjunctive, the amended provision was intended to make the decision to disqualify spousal status more straightforward

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the change from conjunctive to disjunctive test in section 4(1) IRPR to simplify disqualification decisions.

propositions.text: Either element now suffices to disqualify spousal status, making it harder to establish non-disqualification.
propositions.quote: Since either element of section 4(1) of the IRPR will now suffice to disqualify spousal status, it can be more difficult for a spouse to establish that he or she is not disqualified.

propositions.text: Spouse must demonstrate both no immigration purpose and genuineness to avoid disqualification.
propositions.quote: This is because he or she must demonstrate both that the marriage was not entered into primarily for an immigration purpose and that the relationship is genuine

paragraphs.summary: The court states that under the current law, spouses must prove both no immigration purpose and genuineness to avoid disqualification.

propositions.text: Primary purpose test relates to past (time of marriage); genuineness test relates to present (time of decision).
propositions.quote: Under both the previous and the current versions of section 4(1) of the IRPR, the primary purpose test and the genuineness test are determined with respect to different time-frames. The relevant time for the primary purpose test is in the past (i.e. the time of the marriage); the relevant time for the genuineness test is the present (i.e. the time of the decision)

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the primary purpose test applies to the past, genuineness test to the present.

propositions.text: Expectation is officers focus on primary purpose test, but evidence of lack of genuineness is also relevant.
propositions.quote: It is noteworthy that when section 4(1) of the IRPR was amended the expectation was that, in most cases, officers will focus on the primary purpose test. However, “evidence of a lack of genuineness of the relationship is also relevant in examining whether a relationship was entered into for status or a privilege under the Act”

propositions.text: Despite separation of tests, genuineness and immigration purpose can be closely connected in a case.
propositions.quote: Thus, despite the fact that the amended provision separates the primary purpose and genuineness tests and treats each as sufficient in and of itself to warrant a finding that a person is not considered a spouse, there can still be a close connection between the two in a given case.

propositions.text: Evidence of non-genuineness can support inference of immigration purpose and vice versa.
propositions.quote: Evidence that a marriage is not genuine can support the inference that it was entered into primarily for an immigration purpose. The converse is also true.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes officers focus on primary purpose but genuineness evidence remains relevant and the two tests can be connected.

propositions.text: Determinations are difficult; officers must balance family reunification and immigration integrity.
propositions.quote: As the Regulatory Impact Analysis noted, these determinations can be exceedingly difficult. Officers must “proceed cautiously and carefully, ever aware of the need to facilitate family reunification, while at the same time safeguarding the integrity of the immigration process”

propositions.text: Direct evidence of improper purpose is rare; intent inferred from conduct and circumstances.
propositions.quote: There will rarely be direct evidence of an improper purpose. Instead, normally “intent must be inferred from the conduct of the parties and the particular circumstances of the case”

propositions.text: Evidence of genuineness still relevant to adverse conclusions about marriage intentions; failure to consider is reviewable error.
propositions.quote: evidence concerning the genuineness of the marriage can still have a bearing on whether an adverse conclusion about the parties’ intentions when they got married should be drawn ... The failure to consider such evidence can be a reviewable error.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the difficulty of determinations, intent inference, and importance of considering genuineness evidence.

propositions.text: Officer stated Regulation 4 requires marriage to be both not genuine and entered primarily for immigration purpose, reflecting previous version.
propositions.quote: the officer wrote that “Regulation 4 states that a foreign national shall not be considered a spouse of a person if the marriage is not genuine and was entered into primarily for the purpose of acquiring any status or privilege under the Act.”

propositions.text: This is arguably an error but would benefit Mr. Idrizi and officer elsewhere quotes correct version.
propositions.quote: This is arguably an error because it reflects the previous version of section 4(1) of the IRPR, not the current version. However, this would not assist Mr. Idrizi because any such error would have inured to his benefit and, in any event, the officer quotes the correct version of section 4(1) of the IRPR elsewhere.

paragraphs.summary: The officer cited the old version of Regulation 4 but this error benefits the applicant and correct version was also quoted.

propositions.text: Officer focused on cohabitation evidence but failed to make necessary findings linking it to genuineness and immigration purpose.
propositions.quote: having decided to focus on evidence relating to whether Mr. Idrizi and Ms. Ruko were living together, the officer fails to make the findings of fact necessary to tie that evidence to the two questions in issue.

propositions.text: Evidence on cohabitation is relevant to whether marriage was genuine and not for immigration purpose.
propositions.quote: As a matter of logic and common sense, evidence relating to cohabitation is relevant to these questions.

propositions.text: Officer concluded marriage was not genuine and entered primarily for immigration but did not support conclusions with findings of fact.
propositions.quote: The officer found that the spousal status should not be recognized on both grounds ... However, the officer does not make the findings of fact necessary to support these conclusions.

propositions.text: Decision lacks justification, transparency and intelligibility due to missing findings.
propositions.quote: The result is a decision that lacks justification, transparency and intelligibility.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the officer failed to make necessary findings linking cohabitation evidence to key issues, rendering the decision unjustified.

propositions.text: Officer did not expressly find whether parties lived together or link this to marriage intentions.
propositions.quote: The problem is that the officer did not make an express finding that they were not (or had not been) living together or link such a finding to their intentions when they got married.

propositions.text: Officer did not question parties about their intentions at marriage during interview.
propositions.quote: At the interview, the officer did not question Mr. Idrizi or Ms. Ruko at all about their intentions when they got married.

propositions.text: Decision does not explain how cohabitation evidence supports conclusion marriage was for immigration purpose; no other evidence relied on.
propositions.quote: In the decision, the officer does not explain in any way how evidence relating to their cohabitation supported the conclusion that the marriage was entered into primarily for an immigration purpose. No other evidence is relied on for this conclusion.

propositions.text: Decision silent on evidence about parties' immigration and refugee histories that arguably relate to marriage intentions.
propositions.quote: While there was evidence that arguably related more directly to Mr. Idrizi’s and Ms. Ruko’s intentions when they decided to get married (namely, their respective histories under the immigration and refugee process), the decision is silent about it.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the officer failed to make findings on cohabitation or intentions and did not explain how evidence supported conclusions.

propositions.text: Evidence on living arrangements was relevant to genuineness; conflicting evidence existed.
propositions.quote: The evidence concerning Mr. Idrizi’s and Ms. Ruko’s living arrangements was also relevant to the genuineness of their marriage at the present time. There was evidence suggesting that they were not living together, which could support a finding that their marriage is not genuine. There was also evidence suggesting that they were living together, which could support a finding that the marriage is genuine. There was even evidence suggesting that they may have lived together at some times but not at others.

propositions.text: Officer must weigh evidence and make necessary findings; court does not second-guess weighing.
propositions.quote: It was the officer’s role to weigh all this evidence and to make the necessary findings of fact. It is not the reviewing court’s role to second-guess that weighing exercise.

propositions.text: Officer did not make express finding on whether parties lived together but found conflicts sufficient to conclude relationship not genuine.
propositions.quote: However, as noted, the officer never made an express finding that Mr. Idrizi and Ms. Ruko were not living together. Instead, the officer found the conflicts in the evidence on this point to be sufficient to conclude that the relationship is not genuine.

propositions.text: Without finding on living together, foundation for conclusion is uncertain.
propositions.quote: In the absence of a finding of fact on the key question of whether Mr. Idrizi and Ms. Ruko lived together, the foundation for the officer’s ultimate conclusion is uncertain at best.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds conflicting evidence on living arrangements and that the officer failed to make necessary findings, undermining the conclusion.

propositions.text: Mr. Idrizi contends officer erred by relying on inconsistencies about peripheral or honestly mistaken details.
propositions.quote: Mr. Idrizi contends that the officer erred by relying on inconsistencies regarding peripheral details or matters on which someone could be honestly mistaken.

propositions.text: Some inconsistencies may be arguable as errors; others, like meeting parents, are doubtful.
propositions.quote: While this may be arguable in some respects (e.g. the time Mr. Idrizi returned home from work the previous evening), it is very doubtful in others (e.g. whether Mr. Idrizi had met Ms. Ruko’s parents).

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues errors in relying on peripheral inconsistencies; the court finds some arguable, others doubtful.

propositions.text: Officer failed to meaningfully consider evidence favoring genuineness: having a child together.
propositions.quote: the more telling flaw in the decision identified by Mr. Idrizi is the officer’s failure to give any meaningful consideration to evidence that arguably weighed heavily in favour of the genuineness of the marriage – namely, the fact that Mr. Idrizi and Ms. Ruko had had a child together.

propositions.text: Officer asked few inconsequential questions about the child; responses were consistent.
propositions.quote: The officer asked only a few inconsequential questions about the child and whether Mr. Idrizi and Ms. Ruko wanted to have another (to which questions they provided mutually consistent responses).

propositions.text: Existence of child is not determinative but must be considered comprehensively.
propositions.quote: The officer’s conclusory statement that the “existence of a child is not determinative of a positive decision,” while correct, is insufficient.

propositions.text: Officer must set out reasons comprehensibly when dismissing significant evidence; this was not done.
propositions.quote: It was the officer’s responsibility to set them out in a comprehensible way. This was not done.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the officer failed to properly consider the significant evidence of the couple having a child together.

propositions.text: Having a child could support inference marriage not entered primarily for immigration purpose.
propositions.quote: The fact that Mr. Idrizi and Ms. Ruko had had a child together could also support the inference that their marriage was not entered into primarily for an immigration purpose.

propositions.text: Officer did not engage with this question before adverse conclusion on marriage purpose.
propositions.quote: The officer does not engage with this question in any way whatsoever before drawing an adverse conclusion about why Mr. Idrizi and Ms. Ruko got married.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the officer failed to consider how having a child might negate an immigration purpose inference.

propositions.text: Reasons fail Dunsmuir test; do not allow understanding or assessment of decision's acceptability.
propositions.quote: Read as a whole and against the backdrop of the record, the reasons fail the Dunsmuir test. They simply do not allow the reviewing court to understand why the evidence led to the conclusion it did, nor do they permit the court to determine whether this conclusion is within the range of acceptable outcomes.

propositions.text: Court cannot supply reasons or make findings not made by decision-maker.
propositions.quote: It is not for the reviewing court “to supply the reasons that might have been given and make findings of fact that were not made”

propositions.text: Decision must be set aside and matter reconsidered due to lack of adequate reasons.
propositions.quote: As a result, the decision must be set aside and the matter must be reconsidered.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the decision lacks adequate reasons and must be set aside for reconsideration.

propositions.text: Application for judicial review is allowed; officer's decision set aside; matter remitted for redetermination by different officer.
